Unrealized vs realized P&L explained

Unrealized P&L moves with the market on shares you still hold. Realized P&L locks in when you sell. Confusing the two leads to celebrating paper gains that never become cash — or ignoring locked-in losses hiding under a green today number.

By PSX Tracker · Updated 23 September 2026

Unrealized (open positions)

Roughly: market value minus the cost of lots you still hold. It changes whenever prices move and is not cash until you dispose of the position.

A large unrealized gain can vanish in a bad week. Treat it as mark-to-market information, not a bonus already paid.

Realized (closed trades)

Realized results come from sells after cost basis and fees for the lots you closed. They remain in history even if you later repurchase the name.

Realized loss is still a result — ignoring it because you “still believe in the stock” does not erase the closed trade.

Income sits beside both

Dividends are not unrealized share gain and not the same as a sell. Track income separately so Total Return has all three stories: open marks, closed trades and distributions.

How PSX Tracker helps

Holdings views emphasize open lots; realized views emphasize closed trades. Use both when you review performance.

If the two lenses disagree with your memory, trust the ledger — then fix missing trades until memory and ledger converge.

Two questions, two numbers

Unrealized profit asks what the shares or units you still hold are worth against what they cost, at today’s price or NAV. It moves when the market moves, and it is not cash. You cannot spend it, and you have not paid tax on it, because you have not disposed of the position.

Realized profit asks what happened on the sales you already made. Proceeds minus the cost of the lots those sales closed, minus the selling costs you include, is the gain you locked in. It does not change because the price changed tomorrow. Tomorrow is a new day for the shares you still have, not for the shares you sold.

Putting the two numbers in one pot produces a figure with no verb. “I made 50,000” might mean the screen is green or it might mean you sold. The dashboard shows them separately so you can say which one you mean.

How a sale moves the number from one column to the other

Before the sale, the position’s gain is unrealized. When you sell part of it, the lots you closed leave the open book and their gain becomes realized. The shares you kept stay unrealized and keep their own cost. FIFO decides which lots left. Average cost would move a different gain into the realized column from the same sell order.

A sale below cost realizes a loss. That loss is real in the personal ledger even if you do not enjoy looking at it. Hiding it inside a blended average of what you still hold makes the remaining position look worse and the past look cleaner than it was. Keep the loss on the sale.

Fees follow the event. Buy fees sit in the cost of the open lot, so they reduce unrealized profit. Sell fees reduce the proceeds, so they reduce realized profit. Dropping fees from both makes both numbers optimistic.

Cash, income, and transfers are none of the above

A dividend is not unrealized and it is not a capital gain. It is income and, when it arrives, cash. A deposit is not a gain. A withdrawal is not a loss. A transfer of shares to another of your portfolios is not a sale. If any of those land in the realized column, the column stops meaning “I sold something.”

Day-to-day P&L is a third idea again: how the market value changed since the previous close, on the shares you held. It is not the unrealized total, which measures you against your cost, and it is not the realized total, which measures closed trades. A green day can happen while you are still underwater versus cost. A red day can happen while your closed trades for the year are ahead.

Net worth is market value plus cash. It includes unrealized gains because they are inside the market value. It does not add them a second time. If a screen ever seems to count the same profit twice, you are adding a total that already includes it.

Why the broker’s average and your realized figure disagree

Brokers often show one average buy price for the open position. That average is a convenient summary of what you still hold. It does not identify which lots a partial sale closed. Your realized gain can therefore differ from “average times quantity” and both screens can be internally consistent. The contract note plus the lot list is how you see which story you are in.

Tax follows the disposal rules for the year, not the color of the unrealized number. You generally do not file the unrealized figure. You file the disposals, and only under the rules that apply to you. The CGT guide stays at that level on purpose and does not invent a rate.

Fund redemptions realize a result on units. The manager’s statement may already net a tax. Read whether the figure you are copying is before that tax or after it, and do not subtract the tax again.

Use the split when you review the month

Once a month, read one sentence for realized and one for unrealized. Realized: which sales did I make, and do they match the contract notes? Unrealized: which open positions are doing the work, and do I still want them at this size? Mixing the sentences leads to selling a winner to “lock” a feeling, or to ignoring a real loss because the open book is green.

If realized is a large loss and cash is also wrong, reconcile before you draw a lesson about your skill. A duplicated sell can manufacture a loss. A missing deposit can manufacture despair. The numbers are allowed to teach you only after they match the statements.

PSX Tracker keeps the split so the lesson, when you are ready for it, is about your decisions and not about a blended blob. The tool does not grade the decisions.

Common questions

What is unrealized profit?

The gain or loss on shares or units you still hold, using today’s price or NAV against your cost. It changes when the price changes.

What is realized profit?

The gain or loss on a sale you already made, based on the proceeds and the cost of the lots that sale closed.

Why can both numbers be on screen together?

They answer different questions: what the open book is worth versus what closed trades have already locked in.
